title: Online Clipboard with Live Sync — Share Across Devices | Webklip
description: Free online clipboard with live sync. Move text, files, screenshots, and temporary notes between phone and desktop on one private link that expires automatically.
intro: Copy on one device, open the same link on another — text, files, and screenshots stay in sync until the clip expires. No app install, no permanent cloud dump.
paragraphs: An online clipboard is a temporary web workspace you open in any browser. Paste text, drop a file, or press Ctrl+V / Cmd+V for a screenshot, then send the link (or scan the QR code) to your phone, tablet, or a teammate. Every open tab stays connected: edit on your laptop and the same content updates elsewhere in real time — without dumping the payload into Slack, email, or a classic pastebin that sticks around forever.

Webklip is built for that handoff. Clips expire in 15 minutes by default (or longer if you choose), so the bridge between devices does not become another inbox. Use it as a disposable notepad, a live sync clipboard across screens, a temporary file drop, or a QR handoff when typing a long URL on your phone is the last thing you want.

sections.heading: Share text between devices
paragraphs: Stop emailing yourself. Create a clip, paste on one device, open the link on another, and keep both tabs open if you want live updates while you type — verification codes, long URLs, addresses, shopping lists, or a paragraph you are editing across screens.
Unlike a one-shot paste tool, Webklip behaves like a shared notepad: both sides see the same draft until the TTL ends. When you are done, the clip deletes itself instead of living in chat history.

sections.heading: Temporary files and screenshots
paragraphs: Most file-sharing tools create permanent links that linger in cloud storage. Attach an image, PDF, or document to a clip that expires on a schedule — or capture a screenshot, paste it with Ctrl+V / Cmd+V, and send one URL. Recipients preview in the browser; expired clips and their files are cleaned up automatically.
Combine a short note with the attachment on the same page when the picture needs context. That is faster than saving a PNG, uploading to chat, and leaving the image in a channel forever.

sections.heading: QR handoff and temporary notes
paragraphs: Start a clip on your computer, open Share (or the clip QR page), and scan with your phone camera — no retyping long URLs. After the scan, both browsers stay on the same live workspace until expiry.

Use the same flow as a disposable notepad: plain text for scraps, or Markdown when you want lightweight formatting and preview. Nothing is meant to become an archive — just a temporary page that syncs, then disappears.

title: Secure & Private Sharing — E2E, Burn After Read | Webklip
description: Share passwords, credentials, and sensitive notes privately. Passphrase end-to-end encryption, burn-after-read links, and short expiry — without leaving secrets in chat.
intro: Send something sensitive once: encrypt it in the browser, burn it after one view, or let a short TTL clean it up — instead of pasting it into Slack or email forever.
paragraphs: Messaging apps keep permanent copies of whatever you paste — including the password or API key you meant to share once. A secure online clipboard needs more than a random URL: passphrase end-to-end encryption so the server never sees plaintext, burn-after-read for true one-time delivery, and automatic expiry so abandoned secrets do not linger.

Webklip combines those controls in one temporary link. Choose Passphrase in Protect settings to encrypt in the browser before upload; share the clean URL and the passphrase separately. Add burn-after-read when only one real view should count. Pair with a team space when the same handoff happens every week — without turning Webklip into a password manager.

sections.heading: Passphrase end-to-end encryption
paragraphs: With passphrase E2E, content is encrypted in your browser before upload. Webklip stores ciphertext, a public salt, and a wrapped content key only — we never receive your passphrase and cannot decrypt your clip, even if compelled. Recipients unlock locally in the browser.

Memorable phrases are generated by default, or you set your own. Short secrets are allowed with a clear offline-crack warning. Public Klipwall listings cannot use E2E or burn-after-read — those modes stay private by design.

sections.heading: Burn-after-read links
paragraphs: Some information should only be seen once — a password, recovery code, or temporary credential. Burn after read deletes the clip after a single real view: the recipient gets the content, and it is gone.

Paste the link into WhatsApp, Slack, Telegram, or similar apps without worry: their link-preview crawlers see a generic card and do not count as a read, so the clip stays intact until someone opens it in a browser. Keep a short TTL as a backup if nobody opens it.

sections.heading: Passwords, credentials, and teams
paragraphs: Do not drop passwords into chat threads. Put them in a temporary clip with optional E2E and burn-after-read. The same flow works for API keys, Wi-Fi passwords, and recovery codes — share the link (and passphrase) through different channels when you use encryption.

When the handoff happens every week, create a team, invite people by email, and keep clips at webklip.com/team/clip-name. Viewers are read-only; owners and members can edit. Anyone with the link can still open the clip, so passphrase E2E is what actually narrows the audience. Keep long-lived secrets in a vault; use Webklip for the moment a secret has to move, then let it expire. See our security practices for the full model.

title: For Developers — Code Snippets, Markdown & Clipboard API | Webklip
description: Share code snippets with syntax highlighting, paste Markdown with live preview, or automate ephemeral clips with the Webklip REST API and webhooks.
intro: Move code between workstations, preview Markdown on a temporary link, or push short-lived strings from CI — without leaving permanent pastes in chat.
paragraphs: Pasting into Slack or email strips formatting and leaves permanent copies. A classic pastebin leaves a static page online. Developers usually need something in between: a temporary clip with syntax highlighting and live sync for pair review, Markdown preview for release notes, and a plain HTTP API when a script — not a human — needs to pass a one-shot token.

Webklip covers that stack in one product. Paste a snippet, set the language, share the URL; switch to Markdown when notes need structure; or call /api/v1 from curl, CI, or any language. Clips expire by default, support burn-after-read, and can sync live in the browser when humans join the same link.

sections.heading: Share code snippets
paragraphs: Set the language, paste your function or config, and share a URL that syncs while you pair-edit. Syntax highlighting covers dozens of languages. Open it on another monitor or send it to a colleague — changes appear in real time on every open tab.

When the review is done, the clip expires instead of living forever in chat or on a public paste. Combine with a short TTL or burn-after-read when the snippet includes credentials you do not want archived.

sections.heading: Markdown paste with preview
paragraphs: Drop Markdown into a temporary page, use in-browser preview when you want rendered output, and send one URL to another device or a teammate. Keep both sides open to refine the draft live.

Ideal for README fragments, release notes, and checklists that should not become a permanent doc or a flattened Slack message. Add a file or Ctrl+V screenshot beside the Markdown when the note needs an image.

sections.heading: Clipboard REST API
paragraphs: When scripts, CI jobs, or internal tools need to pass a short-lived string, a chat app is the wrong transport. Webklip exposes a JSON HTTP API: create a clip by slug, set a TTL or burn-after-read, read content once, and optionally receive webhooks when a clip is read, burned, or expired.

Anonymous clips need no account. Pair the API with the web UI when humans also open the same link — including live sync — or keep the flow fully automated. Passphrase E2E clips store ciphertext only; decrypt on the client with the passphrase the API never receives. Full reference: REST API and webhooks.

title: Pastebin vs Webklip — Temporary Paste Sharing | Webklip
description: Pastebin vs Webklip: compare permanent pastes with an ephemeral online clipboard that syncs live, attaches files, and expires by default.
intro: Pastebin is built for pastes that stick around. Webklip is an online clipboard built for sharing that disappears — with live sync across every open device.
paragraphs: Pastebin has been the default place to dump code and text for years: create a paste, get a URL, leave it online. That works when you want a long-lived public snippet. It is a weaker fit when you are moving a secret, a one-off config, or a draft between your phone and laptop — the paste often outlives the need, and nothing updates live while you edit.

Webklip takes the opposite default. Paste into a temporary clip, share the link, and every open browser stays in sync until the TTL ends (15 minutes by default). Add files, multiple tabs, passphrase end-to-end encryption, or burn-after-read when you need more than a static paste — without treating every paste as something that should live forever.

title: PrivateBin Alternative — Ephemeral Encrypted Sharing | Webklip
description: Looking for a PrivateBin alternative? Webklip adds live sync, file and screenshot paste, burn-after-read, and expiry by default — with optional passphrase E2E.
intro: PrivateBin encrypts pastes in the browser. Webklip does that too — and keeps every open device in sync until the clip expires.
paragraphs: PrivateBin is a well-known zero-knowledge paste tool: content is encrypted client-side, and you can burn a paste after it is read. That model is excellent for dumping a secret into a static page. It is less ideal when you are actively moving text between phone and laptop, or when you want attachments and live edits on the same link.

Webklip is an online clipboard that behaves like a temporary workspace instead of a one-shot paste. Paste or type into a clip, share the URL (or scan a QR code), and every open tab stays in sync. Turn on passphrase end-to-end encryption when you need zero-knowledge storage, or burn-after-read for single-use secrets — then let the default short TTL clean up what nobody needs anymore.

title: One-Time Secret Alternative — Burn-After-Read Links | Webklip
description: One-Time Secret alternative with burn-after-read, passphrase E2E, live sync, and automatic expiry. Share a secret once — or keep editing until it disappears.
intro: One-Time Secret is built for a single reveal. Webklip can burn after one view too — and also works as a live online clipboard when you need more than a one-shot link.
paragraphs: One-Time Secret (OTS) popularized the idea of a link that self-destructs after it is read. That is perfect for handing someone a password once. The tradeoff is that the page is usually a single retrieval: no ongoing sync, limited room for notes and files, and little help when you are bouncing the same draft between your own devices.

Webklip supports burn-after-read for true one-time secrets, and passphrase end-to-end encryption so the server never sees plaintext. When you do not need a single reveal, use a short TTL instead and keep every open browser in sync — including screenshots pasted with Ctrl+V — until the clip expires.
